name: Mbelime
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.source_named: Neukom, Lukas 2004. Esquisse grammaticale du mbelime, ASAS-Verlag Zurich, 259pp (Glottolog MED grammar); not online. Roberts et al. 2020 Mbelime tone paper on HAL is bot-blocked.

new_statements.quote: The three underlying tone levels in Mbelime are high, mid and low. These underlying tone levels combine to form six underlying tone melodies on noun roots, which I will refer to by their surface representations: L, M, H, S (super high), ML, and LH. [...] Important tonal processes include automatic downstep, high tone raising, and low tone spreading. [p. 3] [...] This alternation may have something to do with stress or phonological phrasing, as well as probable tonelessness of epenthetic vowels (recall that in simple CVCV noun stems, the second vowel is epenthetic). Mbelime speakers only recognize the difference in pronunciation when it is repeatedly pointed out to them. [p. 8]
new_statements.citation: Liu, Rachel. 2013. Tone in Mbelime nouns. Série électronique de documents de travail (SIL Togo-Bénin) 1: 1-45.
new_statements.locator: §1 Introduction, p. 3 (PDF p. 4) and §3.3 'H melody on disyllabic noun roots', p. 8 (PDF p. 9)
new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule for word stress is stated by any accessible source. Mbelime is described first-hand (Liu 2013; Melick 2012) as a three-level tone language (H, M, L, plus a surface super-high) with upstep, automatic downstep and low-tone spread; the only mention of stress is Liu's speculation that a surface-tone alternation on CVCV noun roots might reflect stress or phrasing. Corroborated second-hand by Roberts, Boyd, Merz & Vydrin 2020: 116 ('three contrastive level tones, H, M and L, contour tones, downstep, upstep').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed in any opened source.
new_statements.domain_note: Liu's remark concerns isolation vs phrase-medial realisations of noun tone melodies (citation forms vs phrase); Melick's data are verb forms in frames. Neither addresses a word-stress domain.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the same language (mbel1240, ISO mql, spoken around Cobly, Atacora, Benin). Liu 2013's consultant is from Kountori (living in Cobly); Neukom 2004 was based on four weeks with one speaker from Namounchaga (fieldwork in Kara, Togo); no dialect split is drawn by any source.

sources.note: First-hand tone study (consultant from Kountori, living in Cobly). p. 3: three underlying tone levels H, M, L; six noun-root melodies; automatic downstep, high-tone raising, low-tone spreading. p. 8: a surface H-melody alternation on CVCV roots 'may have something to do with stress or phonological phrasing, as well as probable tonelessness of epenthetic vowels' — a speculation only; no statement of where stress falls or whether Mbelime has word stress.

sources.citation: Melick, Christina M. 2012. Tone in the Mbelime Verb System. MA thesis, Graduate Institute of Applied Linguistics, Dallas (SIL e-Books 47), 144 pp.
sources.access_detail: copy on file; access check: not located online or at Harvard
sources.note: Nothing about Mbelime stress. 'stress' occurs only in the review of Clements' metrical-tree theory of downstep (p. 24) and 'accent' only re Selkirk pitch-accent constraints (p. 101). Ch. 1 (p. 2): 'Mbelime has three underlying tones as well as upstep and downstep'; §4.2 syllable structure (CV, CVV, CVN, CVC, CVCV, CVNCV), §5.1.1 TBU. Her review (pp. 3-6) of Neukom 2005 ch. 2 lists phonemes, syllable structure, tone and processes with no mention of accent; of Hammond & Hamilton 1997 says 'the only mention of tone is simply that there are three levels of tone'.

Consonant and vowel tables sourced to Neukom 2004 pp. 5-7; no tone and no stress statement. Its reference list supplied the Neukom academia.edu link, Rietkerk 2000, Melick 2012, Kombetto et al. 2017 orthography guide.

sources.citation: Roberts, David, Ginger Boyd, Johannes Merz & Valentin Vydrin. 2020. Quantifying written ambiguities in tone languages: A comparative study of Elip, Mbelime, and Eastern Dan. Language Documentation & Conservation 14: 108-138.
sources.note: §5.1 Language overview (p. 116): 14 consonants and 7 vowels (Neukom 2004: 5, 7); 'Mbelime has three contrastive level tones, H, M and L, contour tones, downstep, upstep, and various morphotonological processes (Liu 2013; Melick 2012)'. No mention of stress anywhere in the Mbelime sections.
